ideas.hypothesis: When core cities (e.g., Beijing, Tianjin) tighten environmental regulation, pollution-intensive foreign direct investment moves to neighbouring prefecture-level cities. This produces positive spatial spillovers in dirty-industry FDI and emissions.
ideas.test: Estimate a spatial Durbin panel model for the 52 Bohai Rim cities (2000-2019), with FDI split by industry pollution intensity and regressed on own and neighbours' regulatory stringency (e.g., pollution levy rates).
ideas.disconfirming: Neighbours' regulatory tightening has no effect on a city's inflow of dirty-industry FDI.

ideas.hypothesis: Pollution haven effects in FDI location appear only in dirty industries that are not capital-intensive. In capital-intensive dirty industries, factor-endowment effects dominate and FDI goes to capital-abundant hosts despite stricter regulation.
ideas.test: Use a bilateral industry-level FDI panel and interact host environmental stringency with industry pollution intensity and industry capital intensity in a gravity specification with source-year and industry fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The pollution haven effect is the same regardless of industry capital intensity.

ideas.hypothesis: In resource-dependent developing economies, FDI does less to raise manufacturing productivity, because FDI concentrates in extractive enclaves with few links to manufacturing.
ideas.test: Extend the panel of developing economies used for manufacturing TFP growth regressions, interacting FDI with resource rents as a share of GDP.
ideas.disconfirming: The FDI-TFP effect is no smaller in resource-dependent economies.

ideas.hypothesis: Technology embodied in FDI raises manufacturing productivity more in developing economies with deeper private sector credit, because local firms can finance the investments needed to absorb it.
ideas.test: Regress manufacturing TFP growth in a panel of developing economies on FDI, private credit to GDP and their interaction, with country and period fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction between FDI and private credit is zero or negative.

ideas.hypothesis: Standard time-series Granger tests of FDI's relation with growth and real estate prices are biased because they ignore spatial dependence. Spatial panel Granger tests reverse or remove the inferred causal direction for many cities.
ideas.test: Using a Chinese city panel of FDI, GDP and housing prices, compare city-by-city Granger tests with spatial panel VAR Granger tests that include neighbours' lagged values.
ideas.disconfirming: Spatial and non-spatial Granger tests give the same causal conclusions.

ideas.hypothesis: Foreign direct investment in treaty ports during the late Qing generated industrial spillovers to nearby counties that weakened with distance and are still visible in modern industrialization patterns.
ideas.test: Digitize county-level counts of modern factories (1860-1937) and distances to treaty ports, then estimate spatial regressions of historical and present-day manufacturing intensity on treaty-port proximity.
ideas.disconfirming: Factory presence shows no decline with distance from treaty ports beyond what geography explains.

ideas.hypothesis: Because investors hold on to prior beliefs, FDI shows momentum: previously favoured destinations keep receiving inflows after negative performance shocks, and this asymmetry is stronger after losses than after gains.
ideas.test: Use a bilateral FDI flow panel to estimate how inflows respond to host-country returns or growth surprises, interacted with the source's prior allocation share and the sign of the surprise.
ideas.disconfirming: Inflows respond symmetrically to positive and negative shocks, regardless of prior allocation.

ideas.hypothesis: Special economic zone incentives such as Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor raise FDI in the targeted provinces partly by diverting FDI from neighbouring provinces, a negative spatial spillover.
ideas.test: Run a spatial difference-in-differences on provincial FDI project approvals (2012-2019), comparing the zone, adjacent provinces and distant provinces before and after 2018.
ideas.disconfirming: Adjacent provinces show no decline, or an increase, in FDI relative to distant provinces.

ideas.hypothesis: Countries linked by multinational supply chains, through FDI-induced trade in intermediate goods, show less equity home bias toward each other.
ideas.test: Regress bilateral portfolio equity holdings from coordinated portfolio surveys on bilateral intermediate-goods trade and FDI stocks, with distance and standard gravity controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Supply chain linkages do not predict lower home bias once trade in final goods and distance are controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: Pollution haven effects are strongest in less developed countries that combine high economic freedom with weak environmental institutions, because easy entry plus lax enforcement draws dirty FDI.
ideas.test: In a panel of less developed countries, regress FDI inflows on emissions intensity, interacted with an economic freedom index and environmental-institution indicators, with country fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Economic freedom does not moderate the link between emissions intensity and FDI.

ideas.hypothesis: Resource-dependent emerging economies repatriate a larger share of income to foreign investors relative to cumulative inflows, which adds to current account pressure.
ideas.test: Compute the coverage ratio (income repatriated divided by cumulative inflows) from balance-of-payments data for emerging economies and regress it on resource rents, controlling for FDI stock age.
ideas.disconfirming: Coverage ratios are no higher in resource-dependent economies.

ideas.hypothesis: Manufacturing sectors in host countries that are integrated into multinational supply chains improve eco-efficiency (emissions per unit of output) faster than sectors outside those chains.
ideas.test: Use a country-industry panel combining global value chain participation from input-output tables with sector emissions accounts, and regress emissions intensity on backward participation with fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Supply chain integration has no effect on, or worsens, eco-efficiency.

ideas.hypothesis: Across Chinese prefecture-level cities, FDI inflows were associated with higher sulfur dioxide intensity before the mid-2000s emission controls and with lower intensity afterwards.
ideas.test: Regress city SO2 emissions per unit of GDP on actual utilized FDI in a city panel (2000-2015) from statistical yearbooks, with a post-control-policy interaction and city fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The FDI-SO2 relation keeps the same sign and size before and after the controls.

ideas.hypothesis: Infrastructure development such as high-speed rail links speeds up the convergence of FDI toward secondary cities and away from the dominant core cities.
ideas.test: Run a staggered difference-in-differences on high-speed rail station openings in Bohai Rim cities, using city FDI shares and beta-convergence rates.
ideas.disconfirming: Connected secondary cities do not gain FDI share relative to unconnected ones.

ideas.hypothesis: Regions with more foreign-owned firms develop more local angel investment, because former employees of multinationals build up capital, networks and know-how and then invest in startups.
ideas.test: Regress regional counts of angel deals on lagged foreign affiliate employment, and use investor biographies to test whether angels disproportionately have multinational work histories.
ideas.disconfirming: Foreign affiliate presence does not predict angel activity, and angels are not disproportionately former multinational employees.

ideas.hypothesis: Liberalizing skilled immigration raises later FDI from migrants' origin countries, because diaspora networks lower information costs.
ideas.test: Estimate a bilateral FDI gravity model for Australia and comparable destinations using changes in skilled visa quotas by origin, with migrant stocks instrumented by policy-driven inflows.
ideas.disconfirming: Policy-driven increases in migrant stocks do not raise FDI from origin countries.

ideas.hypothesis: Policy uncertainty in Ukraine delays irreversible greenfield FDI more than reversible mergers and acquisitions, consistent with real-option effects.
ideas.test: Regress quarterly greenfield project announcements and cross-border acquisitions in Ukraine (2005-2019) on a text-based policy uncertainty index, and compare the elasticities.
ideas.disconfirming: Greenfield and acquisition FDI respond equally to uncertainty.

ideas.hypothesis: Generous incentives in the Eastern Economic Corridor attract FDI mostly into upgrading the existing petrochemical cluster rather than into the new target industries, because of path dependence in the cluster.
ideas.test: Compare the sector composition of investment promotion approvals in the zone before and after 2018 with other provinces, using a difference-in-differences by sector.
ideas.disconfirming: Post-2018 FDI growth in the zone is concentrated in the new target industries rather than petrochemicals.

ideas.hypothesis: Euro adoption by new member states increases FDI-driven export diversification, because lower currency risk attracts efficiency-seeking FDI into new product lines.
ideas.test: Build synthetic controls for Slovenia, Slovakia and the Baltic states using an export diversification index and FDI stocks, with donor countries outside the euro area.
ideas.disconfirming: Export diversification and FDI in adopters do not diverge from their synthetic controls after adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: Foreign direct investment in the Queensland real estate market falls when the source currency becomes more volatile against the Australian dollar.
ideas.test: Use foreign real estate investment approvals by source country and quarter, regressed on realized bilateral exchange-rate volatility, with source and time fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Exchange-rate volatility has no effect on real estate FDI approvals.

ideas.hypothesis: In tourist regions such as coastal Croatia, foreign real estate investment raises local real estate prices more than in non-tourist regions.
ideas.test: Regress county-level Croatian price indices and foreign purchase counts on foreign purchases, interacted with tourism intensity (overnight stays per resident), with county fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The price effect of foreign purchases is no larger in tourist counties.

ideas.hypothesis: In African economies, FDI crowds out domestic investment in the same year but crowds it in after two to four years, as supplier linkages form.
ideas.test: Estimate distributed-lag panel regressions of domestic investment on current and lagged FDI for African countries over 1980-2019, with system GMM.
ideas.disconfirming: No sign change across lags, with lagged FDI having zero or negative effects.

ideas.hypothesis: The spread of information and communication technologies weakens the negative effect of geographic distance on bilateral FDI.
ideas.test: Estimate a bilateral FDI gravity model with an interaction between distance and ICT penetration in source and host (internet and broadband rates), using PPML with fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The distance elasticity of FDI does not shrink as ICT penetration rises.

ideas.hypothesis: FDI raises output growth in low-income countries only when domestic savings are above a threshold. Below it, FDI cannot break the poverty trap.
ideas.test: Estimate panel threshold regressions of GDP growth on FDI in low-income countries, with domestic savings to GDP as the threshold variable.
ideas.disconfirming: No significant threshold, with the FDI effect constant across savings levels.

ideas.hypothesis: Emerging economies where FDI is concentrated in the real estate market later see larger current account deterioration, because investment income is repatriated without any matching export capacity.
ideas.test: Use a panel of emerging economies with FDI by sector, regressing the current account balance and investment income outflows five years ahead on the real estate share of FDI stock.
ideas.disconfirming: The real estate share of FDI does not predict later current account deterioration.

ideas.hypothesis: Tariff-jumping FDI triggered by protection raises the productivity of protected domestic firms through competition, offsetting part of the intended benefit of protection.
ideas.test: Use firm-level productivity in industries receiving safeguard or antidumping protection, comparing cases with and without subsequent tariff-jumping FDI in a difference-in-differences.
ideas.disconfirming: Domestic firm productivity does not differ between protected industries with and without tariff-jumping FDI.

ideas.hypothesis: Services FDI and sales of foreign affiliates raise services-sector productivity in sub-Saharan Africa, with bigger gains where sector regulation is lighter.
ideas.test: Build a country-sector panel for sub-Saharan Africa from services trade restrictiveness and FDI stock data, and regress services labour productivity growth on FDI interacted with regulation.
ideas.disconfirming: Services FDI has no productivity effect, regardless of regulation.

ideas.hypothesis: Cooperation between Chinese and foreign investment banks (joint ventures and co-advisory deals) increases foreign firms' entry into China through cross-border acquisitions.
ideas.test: Use a deal database to model the probability of foreign acquirer entry by industry and year, as a function of active Sino-foreign investment bank ventures that advise in that industry.
ideas.disconfirming: Industries with active investment bank cooperation see no more foreign acquisition entry.

ideas.hypothesis: FDI from BRICS countries into Africa repatriates a smaller share of its income and reinvests more than Western FDI, contrary to the view that it simply copies Western practices.
ideas.test: Compare reinvested-earnings shares and repatriation ratios by source country for Angola and other African hosts, using bilateral FDI income statistics.
ideas.disconfirming: BRICS-source FDI repatriates the same share of income as Western-source FDI, or more.

ideas.hypothesis: Country pairs with dense FDI-linked trade networks saw a sharper trade collapse in the Great Recession but recovered faster, because supply chains transmit shocks and then restart together.
ideas.test: Use monthly bilateral trade for 2007-2011 and regress the peak-to-trough drop and the recovery speed on pre-crisis bilateral FDI stocks and intermediate-goods shares.
ideas.disconfirming: Pre-crisis FDI linkages predict neither the size of the collapse nor the speed of recovery.
